metadata.name: Term Database
metadata.description: A central database of IT, networking, and cybersecurity terms with definitions.

terms.definition: Transmission Control Protocol — a connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol that provides flow control, ordering, and error correction.
Internet Protocol — the principal communications protocol for relaying datagrams across network boundaries; provides addressing and routing.
Domain Name System — a hierarchical, decentralised naming system that translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
HyperText Transfer Protocol — an application-layer protocol for transmitting hypermedia documents, the foundation of data communication on the Web.
HTTP Secure — HTTP over TLS/SSL, encrypting the communication channel between client and server.
Transport Layer Security — a cryptographic protocol providing privacy and data integrity between communicating applications.
Cross-Site Scripting — a client-side code injection attack where malicious scripts are injected into trusted websites.
A code injection technique that exploits a vulnerability in an application's database layer by inserting malicious SQL statements into an entry field.
Cross-Site Request Forgery — an attack that tricks a user into performing actions they did not intend, exploiting the trust a site has in their browser.
An open-source platform for developing, shipping, and running applications in lightweight, portable containers.
An open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerised applications.
Application Programming Interface — a set of definitions and protocols for building and integrating application software.
Border Gateway Protocol — the exterior gateway protocol that exchanges routing information between autonomous systems on the Internet.
User Datagram Protocol — a connectionless transport protocol that provides fast, low-overhead communication without guaranteed delivery or ordering.
Secure Sockets Layer — the predecessor to TLS, a deprecated cryptographic protocol for securing communications over a network.
A standard defining the format of public-key certificates used in TLS/SSL, code signing, and email security.
Public Key Infrastructure — the framework of roles, policies, hardware, and software used to create, manage, distribute, use, store, and revoke digital certificates.
Content Security Policy — an HTTP header that lets site operators declare approved sources of content, mitigating XSS and data-injection attacks.
A class of attack in which untrusted input is interpreted as code or commands by an interpreter (e.g. SQL, command, or LDAP injection).
The process of securely maintaining and validating a user's authenticated state across requests, typically using session tokens or cookies.
The process of verifying the identity of a user, device, or system, distinct from authorisation which governs what they may do.
The process of granting or denying a verified identity permission to access resources or perform actions.
Multi-Factor Authentication — an authentication method requiring two or more independent verification factors (something you know, have, or are).
A social-engineering attack that uses deceptive messages to trick victims into revealing credentials, installing malware, or transferring funds.
A lightweight, standalone, executable package that bundles an application with its dependencies and runtime, isolated from the host via kernel namespaces and cgroups.
Open Container Initiative — an open standard defining container image formats and runtime specifications.
The package manager for Kubernetes, using charts to define, install, and upgrade complex Kubernetes applications.
Representational State Transfer — an architectural style for designing networked APIs using stateless HTTP methods and resource-oriented URIs.
A query language and runtime for APIs that lets clients request exactly the data they need, reducing over- and under-fetching.
The process of selecting paths in a network along which to send network traffic, governed by routing protocols and forwarding tables.
A targeted phishing attack directed at a specific individual or organisation, using personalised content to increase success.
Role-Based Access Control — an access-control model that grants permissions to roles, and roles to users, simplifying authorisation management.
Identity and Access Management — the framework of policies and technologies that ensures the right individuals access the right resources at the right time.
A security model that requires continuous verification of every user and device, never trusting anything by default regardless of network location.
Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a routing protocol for Internet Protocol (IP) networks.

Network address translation (NAT) is a method of mapping an IP address space into another by modifying network address information in the IP header of packets while they are in transit across a traffic routing device.

A virtual private network (VPN) is an overlay network that uses network virtualization to extend a private network across a public network, such as the Internet, via the use of encryption and tunneling protocols.

Quality of service (QoS) is the description or measurement of the overall performance of a service, such as a telephony or computer network, or a cloud computing service, particularly the performance seen by the users of the network.

Malware (a portmanteau of malicious software) is any software intentionally designed to cause disruption or destruction to a computer, server, client, or computer network, leak private information, gain unauthorized access to information or systems, deprive access to information, or interfere with…
Ransomware is a type of malware that takes the private data of a victim hostage until a ransom is paid.

In computing, a denial-of-service attack (DoS attack doss) is a cyberattack in which the perpetrator seeks to make a machine or network resource unavailable to its intended users by temporarily or indefinitely disrupting services of a host connected to a network.

In cryptography and computer security, a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, or on-path attack, is a cyberattack where the attacker secretly relays and possibly alters the communications between two parties who believe that they are directly communicating with each other, where in actuality the…
A zero-day (also known as a 0-day) is a vulnerability or security hole in a computer system unknown to its developers or anyone capable of mitigating it.
In cryptography, encryption is the process of transforming information in a way that, ideally, only authorized parties can decode.

Cloud computing is defined by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as "a paradigm for enabling network access to a scalable and elastic pool of shareable physical or virtual resources with self-service provisioning and administration on demand".
Containerization, also referred as container stuffing or container loading, is a system of intermodal freight transport using intermodal containers.

Infrastructure as code (IaC) is the process of managing and provisioning computer data center resources through machine-readable definition files, rather than via physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools.
In computing, load balancing is the process of distributing a set of tasks over a set of resources (computing units) with the aim of making their overall processing more efficient.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is an open standard file format and data interchange format that uses human-readable text to store and transmit data objects consisting of name–value pairs and arrays (or other serializable values).
A regular expression (shortened as regex or regexp), sometimes referred to as a rational expression, is a sequence of characters that specifies a match pattern in text.

Version control (also known as revision control, source control, and source code management) is the software engineering practice of controlling, organizing, and tracking different versions in history of computer files – primarily source code text files, but generally any type of file.
